item.title: Former MLB star calls for salary fix as owners, Players Association talk 'two different languages'
item.description: Nick Swisher warns MLB's collective bargaining negotiation could derail the sport's attendance boom if owners and the Players Association can't agree.
item.content:encoded:
The current collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball and the Players' Association expires in roughly three and a half months, and there seems to be no resolution in sight.

Players are adamant that they will not play under a salary cap, which has been formally proposed by owners for the first time since 1994 — and we all know how that worked out.

"It really does feel like players union and the commissioner's office are speaking two different languages right now," former MLB star Nick Swisher said in a recent interview with Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

It's horrible timing for the game amid a recent boom, as attendance has increased for three consecutive years for the first time since it did each year from 2004 to 2007. In 1995, after a players' strike that cost the '94 postseason, attendance was grim at MLB ballparks.

Swisher, though, has been on both sides of the coin — he won a World Series with the New York Yankees in 2009 and now has a role in their front office as well as the league itself. So, he has advice for both sides.

"I think just in general, the players have a lot of things that they can give, and I think the commissioner's office has some things that they can give, too. So, I think one of the things that I've always realized, especially now being in the business world, is you can't go into a negotiation trying to win. That always ends up bad," he said.

"I'm interested to see how these negotiations are going to come. Are we trying to come to an agreement or are we trying to win the negotiation? So, regardless if it's [MLBPA interim executive director] Bruce Meyer, if it's Rob Manfred in the commissioner's office, I just want the boys to figure it out. Man, we're in such a great spot right now. We need to continue to keep this game going because I don't want it to stop because when it stops, the fans, they get angry about that. All of a sudden, the money starts coming into play and then people don't support us as much anymore. We just need to continue to keep push forward and try and figure out how to make this happen because come 2027, baby, in April, I want to start that season off right."

Players will place blame on small-market teams for not spending money. Those small-market owners, however, will claim they cannot afford big contracts, leaving the superstars to the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees, and a small handful of others. But rather than a cap, Swisher wants to see a salary floor.

BLUE JAYS-RED SOX GAME THROWN INTO CHAOS BY 17-MINUTE 'RULES CHECK,' MASSIVE SCOREBOARD MISTAKE

"You can't have teams paying $60 million a year, because statistically, it shows that those low-market teams don't make it very far into the playoffs. That's just statistics. But I think just in general, if you all of a sudden start bringing that floor into play and then all of a sudden the 22nd, 23rd, 24th, 25th guy on the roster is all of a sudden making some good money, I think that both sides have some things to give and take and I hope that it works itself out," Swisher said.

"We're in a good spot right now. The game is really, really great. Whether you want to blame the commissioner's office, whether you want to blame Players' Association, either way, bro, for me, man, I just want to get it done. Get it done. I don't care who's at fault. I don't care who bets against what. Let's just find a way to get our boys back on the field next year."

Swisher was back on two fields this past weekend - after attending the Yankees' Old Timers' Day in the Bronx, he was in Central Park on behalf of Angry Orchard to surprise one of the worst recreational adult softball teams in the country and play for them to hopefully get a win (they did with the 2010 All-Star).

"To be part of something absolutely new and untraditional, to not only invest in the winners but to invest in the underdogs, bro. They say, don't get angry, get orchard," Swisher said. "Just being able to be part of this and to play with the Sons of Pitches today was absolutely legendary and an epic, man.

"To be able to team up with an organization in a company like Angry Orchard who stands for the right things and wants to invest in everybody. The inclusivity of all of this is something I really enjoy, and to be able to not only handle the winners of the world but to be able to invest in the underdogs too I think is great. So, for me to be part of the underdogs today to pull off a W, it was legendary."

item.title: NCAA has no plans to surrender, as eligibility lawsuits for 2022 class turn into an all-out legal war
item.description: The NCAA announced it will not grant a blanket waiver for the 2022 class, vowing to fight lawsuits over its age-based eligibility rule in court.
item.content:encoded:
During one of the most chaotic periods college athletics has seen when it comes to athlete eligibility, the NCAA made one thing clear Tuesday night: It has no plans to stop fighting the wave of lawsuits coming its way.

Right now, in courtrooms across the country, athletes who were part of the 2022 class are suing the NCAA over what they feel is a misguided and illegal decision that is preventing them from participating this academic year.

When the NCAA adopted its new age-based eligibility model, giving athletes five years to play five seasons, it made one critical decision that is currently being argued on a daily basis: it excluded the 2022 recruiting class from the new rule.

NCAA ROCKED BY COLORADO JUDGE'S 2022 CLASS ELIGIBILITY RULING THAT COULD RESHAPE COLLEGE SPORTS THIS YEAR

Athletes who believe they are being denied an extra season of competition began filing civil lawsuits in courtrooms from Colorado to South Carolina, arguing they should receive the same benefits as those covered under the new eligibility structure.

Now, the NCAA might simply be too deep into this fight to let go of the rope.

Or, perhaps more importantly, the organization understands what could happen if it grants a blanket waiver to every member of the 2022 class who would otherwise have another season of eligibility remaining under the new guidelines if grandfathered in.

Outside courtrooms, some athletic administrators have hinted to Fox News Digital-OutKick that the NCAA's thinking on not granting a blanket waiver or including the 2022 class could center around the fact that there are too many players and not enough roster spots across the country for this to work.

Right now, thanks to an injunction granted by U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney of Colorado, athletes from the class of 2022 were granted the ability to join rosters, provided there was a spot available.

That ruling has already led numerous football and basketball programs to add players who had another year of eligibility under Sweeney's order.

But the NCAA quickly responded, filing an emergency motion for a stay with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, which it mentioned in their hard stance on Tuesday night.

"The Tenth Circuit has ordered an expedited briefing on our request for a stay pending appeal," the NCAA noted about the appeal. The deadline for the class members to file a response to the emergency motion is Friday, August 14.  The NCAA's reply brief must be filed no later than Monday, August 17.  In the meantime, the Wisne injunction remains in effect."

That still left one major question hanging over college athletics: Would the NCAA eventually give in to the pressure and grant a blanket waiver rather than continue fighting lawsuits that have already been filed — and the additional ones still to come?

On Tuesday night, the NCAA delivered its answer.

It's not tapping out.

"The Division I Cabinet, including its student-athlete members, carefully considered whether to make the age-based eligibility rule apply retroactively, and decided that doing so would not be in the best interest of all current and future college athletes," the NCAA announced. "We stand behind and will continue to fully defend the membership's decision.  The injunction should never have been granted, and we have asked the Tenth Circuit to permanently reverse it."

INDIANA TAKES FULL ADVANTAGE OF NCAA COURTROOM CHAOS WITH STUNNING ROSTER MOVE AMID ELIGIBILITY FIGHT

And beyond the potentially massive ramifications of the Tenth Circuit's eventual decision, confusion remains over another important issue: Which athletes are allowed to enter the transfer portal?

On Tuesday night, attorney Ryan Downton noted to Fox News Digital-OutKick that a vast number of coaches he has spoken with during this process are siding with the athletes.

"The NCAA keeps calling it "the Membership’s decision" to exclude the Class of 2022," Downton noted. "But neither the NCAA schools nor the coaches got to vote on this proposal. The overwhelming majority of coaches I talk with want these kids to have a chance to play."

In states such as Tennessee and Ohio, injunctions granted in separate cases allow players who are plaintiffs in those lawsuits to use the transfer portal.

But in the Colorado case that athletic departments across the country are closely watching, the plaintiffs have not been granted an additional portal window.

The opinion of some is that the organization knew that implementing its new eligibility rule in June — rather than before the last portal window for each sport — could trigger a wave of lawsuits from athletes who suddenly found themselves on the wrong side of the new guidelines.

The roots of the current fight can be traced back to the Diego Pavia case and, maybe more importantly in the future, former Vanderbilt linebacker Langston Patterson's lawsuit against the NCAA in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee.

Patterson is currently challenging the NCAA over the number of years athletes are allowed to participate in college athletics.

And the concept behind the NCAA's new "age-based eligibility" rule had already been presented in court.

Attorney Ryan Downton, who represents Patterson and athletes in more recent lawsuits filed after the NCAA implemented its new eligibility rule, previously argued for what became known as the "five-for-five" model.

"We asked the NCAA to give everyone five years last year when we filed the Patterson lawsuit. They said no," Downton told Fox News Digital-OutKick last week.

"Now they’ve done it, but excluded the athletes asking for the change. It feels like the NCAA is saying, ‘you had a good idea, but we can’t let you enjoy the benefits of it.’ Just like they changed the name. We called it ‘five-for-five.’ They call it ‘age-based eligibility.’ It’s the same thing, but the NCAA tries to pretend it isn’t."

That's the part of this fight that will continue to fuel frustration among members of the 2022 class.

They wanted five years to play five seasons. The NCAA ultimately adopted a system that does essentially that. But the athletes who were already pushing for the change were left out.

Now, the NCAA has drawn a line in the sand and appears prepared to defend its stance across multiple states, with its most recent loss coming on Tuesday in a Texas courtroom.

Maybe the organization believes that refusing to make the rule retroactive is genuinely the right thing to do.

Or maybe NCAA officials understand they have little choice, given the potential fallout that could come with granting a blanket waiver and opening thousands of additional roster spots that don't actually exist.

Either way, the NCAA isn't waving the white flag.

And now, we wait on an appeals court in Colorado to deliver what will ultimately be a monumental decision.

item.title: Spanberger’s rough rural reception draws Hillary Clinton parallels
item.description: Del. Wren Williams compared Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's Galax visit to Hillary Clinton's hot sauce moment, saying nobody was buying it.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger was roasted for her visit to a nearly century-old fiddling convention in southwestern Virginia, with the area’s state delegate comparing her unfavorably to failed presidential candidate Hillary Rodham Clinton.

Clinton famously surprised the hosts of New York’s "Breakfast Club" radio program in 2016 when she said she regularly carries hot sauce in her purse — a remark critics said echoed Beyoncé Knowles and amounted to political pandering to Southern and Black voters during her 2016 race against then-businessman and reality TV star Donald Trump.

Del. Wren Williams, a Republican who represents Galax, where the 90th Annual Old Fiddlers’ Convention took place, told Fox News Digital he was proud of constituents who made their feelings about the governor known peacefully but strongly.

DEM GOVERNOR BOOED AT VIRGINIA OLD FIDDLERS' CONVENTION

Williams said it was clear to those assembled that Spanberger was trying to "pander" to rural residents, who have pushed back on several of the governor’s priorities, including the judicially halted redistricting effort and a slew of what Richmond Republican leaders have called "the bad bills."

"[It was] about like Hillary Clinton and her hot sauce – nobody was buying it," Williams said.

Over the weekend, Spanberger and her public safety chief, Galax native Stanley Meador, were booed after Meador introduced the governor. Meador previously served as special agent in charge of the FBI’s Richmond Field Office during the "anti-Catholic memo" controversy that drew congressional scrutiny.

Williams told Fox News Digital that people in Galax and surrounding Carroll County — atop the Blue Ridge and just over the border from Andy Griffith’s "Mount Pilot" area of North Carolina — have felt ignored by Spanberger and said their reaction was justified.

SUPREME COURT DEALS BLOW TO VIRGINIA DEMOCRATS IN FIGHT OVER STATE COURT ELECTION MAP RULING

"These are my constituents, the same ones that she just disarmed, tried to force into one single congressional district that represented their political views, and lied every step of the way while jockeying for the national Democratic Party nod for her shot at first female president," Williams said, referring to another parallel between Spanberger and Clinton.

Galax, currently represented in Congress by Rep. Morgan Griffith, R-Va., would have sat at the edge of the only remaining Republican-held district under Richmond Democrats’ proposed 10-1 congressional map, which a bipartisan group of Virginia Supreme Court justices blocked earlier this year.

Virginia's top state Republican – whose district is not far west of where Spanberger got booed – told Fox News Digital the incident proved to the governor that her policies run counter to what his neighbors want from Richmond:

"Southwest Virginians have never been shy about standing up for their values and their way of life," said House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore of Gate City.

"When you try to take away their voice in Congress, go after their Second Amendment rights, and drive up their power bills to pay for a green energy agenda they don’t want and can’t afford, folks are going to let you know how they feel," he said.

Former Attorney General Jason Miyares, a top figure in the "Vote No" coalition opposing Spanberger’s redistricting effort, said in a statement that the crowd’s response was predictable.

"Governor Spanberger booed in Galax. Turns out when you break your campaign promise, attempt a leftist power grab pushing an unconstitutional gerrymandering effort In order to silence rural Virginia voices, coupled with massive tax increases, it results in a frosty reception," Miyares said.

WATCH: SPANBERGER KNOCKED FOR ‘BAIT AND SWITCH’ HYPOCRISY AS POPULARITY PLUMMETS AMID REDISTRICTING FIASCO

"Spanberger finally had to face the music," another Virginia user wrote on X.

Other critics contrasted Democrats’ strength in Northern Virginia with opposition to Spanberger in more rural parts of the state.

"These folks booing are showing how the vast majority of those of us in Virginia feel… not those communists in the blue suburbs of DC," Diane Cheesbrough wrote on X.

"She needs to go and take Tim Kaine and Mark Warner and Eugene Vindman with her."

TRUMP BLASTS SPANBERGER AHEAD OF VIRGINIA MEETINGS, SAYS STATE FACES TAX BASE EXODUS LIKE NEW YORK, CALIFORNIA

Radio host Scott Adams added that rural voters "are not forgetting" the redistricting controversy.

"Southwest Virginia just delivered the message in person," he said.

"Virginians are done with her," added former Rep. Matt Gaetz, R-Fla.

Some observers, however, credited Spanberger with going to Galax and Carroll County despite her weak electoral support in the area.

VIRGINIA VOTERS CEMENT SWING DISTRICT REMATCH AFTER DEMS’ REDISTRICTING FAIL

"Abigail Spanberger lost [the independent city of] Galax 68 to 32 and showed up anyway," said Democratic strategist Matt Royer.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"A Republican would have tucked tail and stayed at home when it comes to events in places they lost, like Jason was yesterday. She won Virginia by 15 and still went to one place that booed her. That is the job."

Fox News Digital reached out to Spanberger and Clinton for comment.

item.title: Three school safety steps every parent should know before classes begin
item.description: A parent outlines three essential back-to-school safety steps, from demanding emergency training for educators to evaluating personal safety tools.
item.content:encoded:
I reviewed my children’s back-to-school shopping lists last week. After wrapping my head around the dizzying array of required items, I was struck by what was missing: safety.

Across America, parents will spend the next few weeks buying everything from notebooks, pens, and pencils to dorm fridges, shower caddies, and laundry baskets.

No parent wants their child to be "that kid" — the one who accidentally shows up on the first day with the wrong calculator or without gym shoes. Yet whether dropping them off at the bus stop or at the quad, almost none of them will send them away with an honest, practical conversation about safety — the one thing they need most.

IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?

Why? Sometimes, because we assume our kids already know what to do or that someone else will teach them. Mostly because it’s uncomfortable. It’s easier to talk about spiral notebooks and extra-long twin sheets than about what to do if the unthinkable happens. But silence has not made our schools safer — and it has not made our children more prepared.

Real back-to-school readiness means facing potential threats head-on. As parents gear up for the school year, there are three essential steps they should take.

1. Demand that educators be trained and equipped for an emergency.

Teachers and other school staff are often the first line of defense in a crisis. That’s an enormous responsibility for people whose emergency training is often little more than a checklist and an afternoon seminar. This is not a knock on teachers and staff. It’s a gap in what schools have been asked and funded to provide.

Genuine school safety requires much more than a plan on paper. It means a strong physical footprint (single-point entry, rapid classroom door locks), modern safety tools (mass notification system, AI-assisted surveillance), and emergency training. Parents shouldn’t hesitate to ask direct questions. How are teachers trained? What safety tools are actually available in the classrooms? How quickly can the school communicate with families during an emergency? Teachers and staff deserve real support, and parents deserve transparency.

2. Talk about safety early — and often.

It’s a natural human instinct to want to shield a seven-year-old from a worry they haven’t asked for or to protect a college freshman’s first weeks from worst-case scenarios. I feel that pull every fall. But while it’s natural, it doesn’t protect our children from risk.

The goal isn’t to scare children. It’s to prepare them — to build awareness, confidence, and the ability to respond if something ever goes wrong. As parents, we can’t shy away from these discussions.

WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO

Obviously, what you say should be age-appropriate. The message you give a second-grader shouldn’t sound like the one you give a high school senior or college freshman.

For my wife and me, this meant walking through our kids’ schools ourselves, understanding the layout and emergency plans, then sitting down with our kids and having the conversation more than once. It’s not a one-time "big talk." It’s something we bring up naturally before school starts and revisit throughout the year. We remind them to pay attention to their surroundings, trust their instincts, and know what to do if something feels wrong.

Will older kids roll their eyes? Of course. "Yeah, mom. Yeah, dad. I know." That’s part of parenting. Say it anyway. Sometimes, the things our kids hear for the hundredth time are the things they remember when it matters most. And if they’re ever faced with danger, there’s a good chance they’ll remember exactly what you told them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The same approach applies online. First-day-of-school photos are a tradition in our home, like many others. But we’ve started thinking twice before posting them. Sharing a school’s name, a daily routine, or a child’s interests online creates unnecessary exposure. Teaching our kids to pause before they post has become another safety habit we’re trying to build.

3. Evaluate appropriate personal safety tools.

Everyone has the right to feel safe, and families should take full advantage of every lawful tool their school or college permits. Families should familiarize themselves with campus policies and equip their students with the protective options they’re comfortable carrying. Depending on a student’s age and school policy, those options range from personal safety alarms to ballistic backpack inserts.

For college students, families should review campus safety policies and consider permitted personal safety tools — such as noise alarms, location-sharing emergency apps, and, where allowed by university policy, standard pepper spray. Faculty should consider other non-lethal options with greater range and stopping power.

We insure our homes against fires that may never happen. We buckle seat belts hoping they’ll never be needed. Preparing our children for a school emergency is no different. We all pray they’ll never have to use what we’ve taught them. But hope has never been a safety plan.

We can’t control every danger our children may face. We can control whether we’ve prepared them for it. That’s a responsibility no parent should leave to chance.

item.title: Trump-backed Michael Alfonso wins crowded GOP primary for his father-in-law's former Wisconsin seat
item.description: Michael Alfonso, Sean Duffy's 26-year-old son-in-law, defeated a crowded field to win the Republican nomination for Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District.
item.content:encoded:
Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy, has won the Republican Party’s nomination in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District.

The 26-year-old, endorsed by President Donald Trump, defeated a crowded field of contenders as he seeks the same northern Wisconsin congressional seat once held by his father-in-law, who represented the district from 2011 to 2019.

"It is my Great Honor to endorse MAGA Warrior, Michael Alfonso, a young ‘STAR’ who is running to represent the incredible people of Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District," Trump wrote on Truth Social on the eve of Tuesday’s Election Day.

"As your next Congressman, Michael will work tirelessly to Grow our Economy, Cut Taxes and Regulations, Champion our Amazing Farmers and Ranchers, Promote MADE IN THE U.S.A., Unleash American Energy DOMINANCE, Keep our Border SECURE, Stop Migrant Crime, Support our Military/Veterans, Safeguard our Elections, and Protect our always under siege Second Amendment," Trump added.

DEMOCRAT ESTABLISHMENT STRIKES BACK AS SOCIALIST CANDIDATE DOWNED IN BATTLEGROUND PRIMARY

The seat is currently held by Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., who on Tuesday won the Republican nomination in the Wisconsin governor’s race.

Tiffany was first elected to the seat in a May 2020 special election after Duffy resigned due to one of his children's health issues.

District 7 has been under control of Republicans for 15 years, and it is deemed a solid Republican by Cook Political Report. Trump carried the district with about 60% of the vote during the 2024 presidential election.

NEW MIDTERM BATLEGROUND TAKES SHAPE AS PARTIES BUILD ELECTION ARMIES

Alfonso will face off against Fred Clark in November, who won Tuesday’s Democratic primary for Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District.

Clark, a former Wisconsin state assemblyman, said on his website that he believes northern Wisconsin has the "makings of a new rural majority."

"That’s a majority not based on old right wing and left wing politics, but a majority made up of real people who live and work in our communities," Clark’s website said. "Fred Clark will become part of a new majority of leaders in Congress who will stand up, represent their communities, and do the work we expect from our elected representatives."

Fox News Digital’s Elaine Mallon contributed to this report.

item.title: Caitlin Clark felt 'sick' hearing Fever fans boo head coach Stephanie White following her pregame rant
item.description: Caitlin Clark said it made her "a little sick" when Indiana Fever fans booed head coach Stephanie White during pregame introductions Tuesday night.
item.content:encoded:
Entering Tuesday's WNBA action, the Indiana Fever sat tied atop the Eastern Conference standings at 20-12 on the year. The team also happens to lead the league in points scored per game with the two-headed monster of Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark leading the charge.

Overall, things should be pretty great for Fever head coach Stephanie White and her squad with the WNBA playoffs in sight.

In reality, the situation in Indiana is completely unsettled, and White was reminded of that on Tuesday night when some fans booed her during pregame introductions ahead of the Fever's home contest against the New York Liberty.

FEVER COACH STEPHANIE WHITE LAUNCHES FIERY DEFENSE OF HERSELF AFTER SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM HIT

Clark addressed the boos her head coach received during her postgame press conference following Indiana's 106-92 win, and she was none too pleased.

"I hated that our fans booed her before the game," Clark explained. "That made me a little sick, to be honest. We're going to ride for her, and we're always going to have her back," Clark continued. "That's never going to tear our locker room apart."

White hearing some boos while being introduced in her own team's building came shortly after she delivered quite the pregame rant about Indiana's Sophie Cunningham and the hard foul she took over the weekend from Chicago's DiJonai Carrington, and the overall boiling tensions around the league.

White explained Tuesday that she didn't, in real time, get to see replays of the foul that left Cunningham with a bloody mouth and Carrington being ejected from the game before going directly to her postgame press conference.

"Was it egregious? Absolutely," White said. "When you have a chance to watch that over and over and over on replay, you can see that. I didn't have that in real time."

CAITLIN CLARK, KELSEY MITCHELL POWER FEVER PAST LIBERTY, LIFT INDIANA ATOP EASTERN CONFERENCE

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win," White said. "It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided."

White closed out her pregame presser on Tuesday by saying critics can "go to hell."

"Love will win, grace will win. Humility will win, and kindness will win. I stand by them, I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell," an emotional White said.

While White admitted that she wasn't able to see replays of Carrington's Flagrant 2 foul on Cunningham from the Fever's game against the Sky on Saturday, that didn't stop her from essentially defending Carrington during her postgame press conference following the contest on Aug. 8.

item.title: Fake rental listing scams can cost you thousands
item.description: FBI real estate fraud complaints jumped from 9,359 in 2024 to 12,368 in 2025 as fake rental listing scams grow more convincing with stolen photos.
item.content:encoded:
You find a charming rental in the right neighborhood. The price sits slightly below other homes nearby. Better yet, it becomes available right when your current lease ends. Then the pressure begins. Consider a Southern California renter who recently found a two-bedroom bungalow near family. The supposed landlord said she could not tour it because the current occupants had not moved out. Instead, he sent her a professional video of the home.

The video looked convincing because it was real. However, the scammer had copied it from an earlier property listing. After collecting an application fee, the fake landlord requested a deposit through Zelle. A phone conversation helped ease the renter's concerns. He also promised receipts and said the deposit was refundable.

She sent more than $2,500. When she asked for the money back, the calls stopped and the messages went unanswered. The actual homeowner still lived in the house and had never offered it for rent. That experience shows how quickly fake rental listing scams can turn a hopeful move into a financial crisis.

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.

WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME

Rental scams have been around for years. However, criminals now have more places to reach people who need housing quickly. Fake listings can appear on established real estate websites. They also circulate through Facebook, TikTok and other social platforms with less oversight. That wider reach gives scammers access to renters who feel worn down by rising prices and fierce competition. When an affordable home appears, people may worry that taking an extra day to investigate will cost them the opportunity. Criminals count on that reaction.

The FBI received 12,368 real estate fraud complaints in 2025. That was up from 9,359 complaints in 2024. Reported losses climbed from about $174 million to more than $275 million. The FBI category covers more than fake rental advertisements. Still, the jump shows how much money people are losing through property-related fraud.

CyberGuy has previously covered how rental scams work and what renters should watch for. Today's fake listings can look even more convincing because scammers have access to professional property photos, video tours and AI tools.

Many scammers do not need to invent a property. Instead, they steal an existing listing. They copy the photos and property description. They may also download a real estate agent's video tour. Then they replace the contact details and post the home on another website or social platform. When you respond, every message goes directly to the scammer.

The Federal Trade Commission says criminals may collect application fees or deposits from several people before anyone discovers the property was never available. They may also use rental applications to steal sensitive information such as a Social Security number or driver's license image. Artificial intelligence can make the operation look more polished. A scammer can use it to improve awkward messages or create professional-looking documents. However, many scams still rely on copied photos and a believable excuse. The FBI recorded 115 real estate fraud complaints that referenced AI during 2025. Those complaints reported nearly $2.7 million in losses. That does not mean AI powered most rental fraud. However, it shows that the technology has become part of some real estate schemes.

FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS

Rental scammers understand timing. You might need to move before school starts. Your lease may expire soon. Perhaps you found a home closer to work or family. When the market feels competitive, waiting can seem like losing your chance. Scammers use that pressure to keep you moving forward.

First, they explain why you cannot tour the property. Then they provide a video that appears to answer your concerns. If you question the payment recipient, they may claim that the person handles applications. Each answer sounds possible on its own. A phone call can also create false confidence. Hearing a real voice proves that a person exists. It does not prove that the person owns the home. Likewise, a video proves that somebody filmed the property. It does not prove that your contact can rent it to you. The FTC warns that even a virtual tour cannot guarantee that a home is available.

Watch closely when the rent falls far below similar homes nearby. A small discount may seem reasonable. A bargain combined with immediate pressure deserves more scrutiny. You should also pause if the landlord refuses an in-person tour. Scammers often blame current tenants or an unexpected trip. They may tell you to drive past the home instead.

Another warning appears when a listing vanishes, but the supposed landlord continues contacting you privately. A scammer may claim the ad attracted too many applicants. In reality, the platform may have removed it. Be cautious when the payment recipient has a different name. Claims involving an assistant or secretary require independent verification. Finally, walk away when someone demands money before you confirm who owns or manages the home. A professional video and friendly conversation do not replace that step.

A little extra checking can protect your moving budget and your identity.

Search the full address using more than one search engine. Look for older sales pages and active rental advertisements. Compare the photos, monthly rent and contact details. If another agent or property management company appears, contact it directly. Use the number on the company's official website rather than one supplied by the person texting you. Also, search the owner's or property manager's name with terms such as "scam," "complaint" or "review." The FTC recommends this step when checking a rental.

Use Google Lens or another reverse-image tool to see where the property photos appeared before. You may discover that the home recently sold or that the images belong to an unrelated listing. CyberGuy's guide explains how to reverse-search an image on your phone. Still, finding only one version of a photo does not guarantee the advertisement is legitimate. The original page may no longer be online.

Visit the home and step inside before sending an application fee or deposit. When you cannot go yourself, ask a trusted friend to attend the showing. A live video call can provide more confidence than a prerecorded tour, but you should still verify the person conducting it. The FTC advises renters to keep looking when a landlord insists on collecting money before showing the property.

Check the county assessor's property records for the owner's name. Keep in mind that these records may not reflect a very recent sale. Then ask the landlord for identification and documentation showing that the person can rent the property. For an apartment building, call the leasing office directly. Do not use a phone number from an unexpected text or social media message.

A scammer may use the name and photo of a real estate agent. Search for that agent's official brokerage page. Then call the office number shown there and ask about the rental. Do not rely on a profile or phone number supplied within the advertisement.

Payment apps make sending money easy. Unfortunately, an authorized payment can be difficult to reverse. Before using Zelle, confirm that the recipient is someone you know and trust. Learn more about the warning signs in CyberGuy's guide on how to avoid getting scammed on Zelle. Also, avoid anyone who demands gift cards, cryptocurrency or a wire transfer. Those methods give scammers a better chance of disappearing with your money. When a legitimate rental company accepts credit cards, that option may offer stronger dispute protections than a peer-to-peer payment.

Do not send your Social Security number or driver's license until you verify the property and landlord. Be cautious when someone directs you to a credit-check website through a texted link. The page could collect your personal information or payment card details. Instead, ask which screening company handles the application. Then find that company's official website yourself.

A polished profile does not prove someone is a legitimate landlord. Look at when the account was created. Review its earlier posts and check whether real people interact with it. You should also watch for copied profile pictures or an account that suddenly changed names. CyberGuy's guide to protecting yourself from social media scammers includes more ways to evaluate suspicious accounts.

Scammers want you to believe this rental is your only chance. It isn’t. Walking away from an affordable home can feel frustrating, especially after weeks of searching. However, losing thousands of dollars could leave you unable to secure the next legitimate rental.

If you sent money to a fake landlord, act quickly to protect your finances and improve your chance of recovery.

Fake rental listing scams succeed because criminals borrow real property advertisements and add a story that explains why you cannot tour. The strongest defense is verification. Confirm who owns or manages the home before you complete an application or send money. Also, do not let a deadline silence your instincts. A caller can sound friendly while using stolen photos and a fake lease. When something feels wrong, pause and check the address through an independent source. That brief delay could protect your savings and your identity.

Have you ever nearly fallen for a rental scam or spotted one before sending money? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Trump brushes off reporter question about running for third term in 2028: 'The law is very strong'
item.description: President Donald Trump told reporters "the law is very strong" on a third term but has previously outlined a JD Vance route scholars reject.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump dismissed a question Tuesday night from a reporter about the possibility of him running for a third term in 2028, saying "the law is very strong."

"Everybody asks me that question, and you know that the law is very strong on that," Trump said while speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. "I'd love to run, but the law is very strong."

"I get asked by everyone, well, even tonight they're screaming at the event, '2028,'" he said, referring to the Patriot Games, which he had attended earlier that day. "No, everybody wants me to do it, but the law is very strong."

Section 1 of the 22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution states that no one can be elected president more than twice.

TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028

The amendment was ratified by the states in February 1951, roughly six years after the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt, who had served an unprecedented four terms as president.

Before Roosevelt, it was a longstanding political norm for presidents to serve no more than two terms, following the precedent set by George Washington.

Throughout his second term, Trump has walked a fine line between joking about seeking a third term and signaling that he may be serious about the idea.

At the White House Correspondents' Dinner on July 24, Trump opened his speech with a wisecrack about running again.

TRUMP HEADS BACK TO CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER MONTHS AFTER GUNFIRE FORCED EVACUATION

"Just like my presidency, the second time is always better. It's always better. And the third time will be better yet. I'm only kidding," Trump said.

In an interview on March 30, 2025, with NBC’s Kristen Welker, Trump struck a different chord, explicitly saying he was not "joking" about seeking a third term.

"There are methods which you could do it," he also told Welker, acknowledging one possible route in which Vice President JD Vance could run for president with Trump as his running mate, win, and then resign — allowing Trump, as vice president, to succeed him and potentially sidestep the 22nd Amendment’s prohibition on being elected president more than twice.

Most constitutional scholars say this would not work. Deborah Pearlstein, a Princeton University law professor, told The Washington Post that the 12th Amendment "closes the door" on Trump securing a third term through the vice presidency.

The amendment’s final sentence states that "no person constitutionally ineligible to the office of President shall be eligible to that of Vice-President of the United States."

item.description: The coastal town of Saint-Tropez is "packed" as influencers drive more tourists to the French Riviera. A luxury travel influencer shared tips for anyone wanting to avoid crowds.
item.content:encoded:
A once-glamorous coastal town on the French Riviera is losing its luster, many tourists say. 

Long known as a playground for celebrities and the ultrarich, Saint-Tropez has found a new audience: influencers who showcase its designer shops and picturesque waterfront.

Luxury travel influencer JQ Louise, who has been visiting Saint-Tropez for 15 years, told Fox News Digital in an interview that the destination is "packed."

POPULAR VACATION HOT SPOTS SLAP LIMITS ON TOURIST RENTALS, DRIVING AND MORE TO PROTECT 'STUNNING' SPACES

"I think influencers have really captured how picturesque it is," said Louise, who is based in Boston. "Saint-Tropez is a dream destination."

But that exposure comes with a downside, Louise said — particularly during the height of summer.

"If you go in June, July or August — and particularly July and August — Saint-Tropez is packed," she said, adding that visitors could find themselves "shoulder to shoulder" with crowds at the port, popular cafés and beach clubs.

Once a quiet Mediterranean fishing village, Saint-Tropez exploded into a global hot spot in the 1950s, sparking a massive, decades-long surge in tourism, the National Geographic reported.

Today, the town of just 4,000 permanent residents is stretched to its absolute breaking point, absorbing up to 80,000 daily visitors during the July and August rush, the Saint-Tropez Tourism Office noted.

The sheer volume of summer crowds has become so unsustainable that the mayor, Sylvie Siri, is now publicly pleading with travelers to visit during the off-season instead, according to the BBC.

POPULAR DESTINATION CRACKS DOWN HARD ON TOURISTS AS NEW LIMITS THREATEN SUMMER GETAWAYS

On a Reddit forum dedicated to luxury travel, one traveler recently asked whether the French Riviera was even worth it.

In response, many were quick to voice their frustrations with the popular vacation spot.

"It's a scene, and overcrowded, definitely NOT my definition of vacation," one person wrote. "Expensive does not [equal] luxury for me."

"The crowd has become almost unbearable," another said.

"Saint-Tropez isn’t for tourists. It’s for residents," another person said, citing its limited appeal and accessibility for ordinary visitors.

"Just because it has this aura of 'old money' and rappers singing about it doesn’t mean it’s good for visitors. It’s for locals who have houses there," the user added.

ONCE-AFFORDABLE SUMMER ESCAPE ROCKED BY SOARING COSTS AS FAMILIES SHELL OUT THOUSANDS

"Going there just to say you are vacationing in Saint-Tropez is dumb considering how difficult it is to get there as a tourist, unless you have a car."

Others were quick to defend the popular vacation spot.

"The Riviera is unreasonably beautiful, and the high-end resorts know how to do hospitality well."

Louise said timing can make a big difference for travelers who want to avoid crowds.

"Try to go in the shoulder season," she said, referencing those who feel it's worth it. "Avoid July and August. It’s too packed." She said she prefers September, October, April and May.

She also said there are plenty of other places in the Riviera to visit "that are just as beautiful, if not more beautiful."

"I love to tell people to pick a place as a home base, then plan kind of a few day trips or plan a few side trips as part of your vacation," she said.

"Whether you're staying in Saint-Tropez or if you're staying in Cannes or Monaco or Nice, there are so many villages all along the Riviera and honestly, they're all beautiful," Louise said.

"Most of them are not crowded even in peak season. I would say go a little bit more on the road less traveled."

item.title: AMBASSADOR GEORGE DEEK: The Christian Israel you are not being shown
item.description: Israel's envoy to the Christian world, raised Greek Orthodox in Jaffa, says Christians grew from 34,000 in 1950 to 184,000 and continue to flourish.
item.content:encoded:
I grew up in Jaffa, going to church every Sunday with my father, the cantor of our Greek Orthodox church. I joined the Christian Scouts as a boy, later became a leader in the movement and even ran our marching band, a serious source of community pride. We marched at Christmas and Easter. We celebrated weddings, baptisms and feast days. We knew which grandmother made the best food and which family was feuding with which other family.

In other words, we were a perfectly normal Middle Eastern Christian community. Our neighbors were Muslims and Jews. We studied together, worked together, argued together and lived together.

I grew up Christian, Arab and Israeli. I felt rooted, safe and happy. Which is why I sometimes wonder whether the Israel I keep reading about is a different country.

THE WAR ON AMERICA’S JUDEO-CHRISTIAN ROOTS THREATENS EVERYTHING WE SHARE

Apparently, Christians here live under siege, Christianity is being pushed out, and Jewish hostility is making Christian life increasingly impossible. It is an alarming picture, and a very strange description of the country in which I actually live.

Let me make one thing clear: There have been ugly incidents of religious radicals spitting at clergy, verbally abusing Christians and vandalizing property. Such behavior is disgraceful. Israel should confront it forcefully through law enforcement, education and religious leadership.

But then comes the question that strangely disappears from much of the discussion:

Do those extremists define Israel? Because if they do, we are going to have to rewrite our descriptions of quite a few Western democracies.

In 2025, the Anti-Defamation League recorded 6,274 antisemitic incidents in the United States, an average of 17 every day. More significantly, there were 203 physical assaults, the highest number the ADL has recorded since it began tracking such incidents.

Does that make America an antisemitic society? Of course not.

Then there is Spain.

According to Spain's Interior Ministry, hate crimes and hate incidents reached their highest recorded level in 2025, rising 23.6% in a single year. Antisemitic incidents rose 86.5% from 37 to 69 cases.

Should we therefore conclude that Spain itself is fundamentally anti-Jewish? Again, no.

ISRAEL LAUNCHES 'BIBLICAL HIGHWAY' AMID CAMPAIGN TO ERASE JEWISH HISTORY

Extremism exists in every democratic society. Sometimes it grows dangerously. Governments must confront it. But serious people understand the difference between extremists within a society and the character of the society itself.

Except, increasingly, when that society is Israel.

An extremist in Boston, Madrid or London attacks a Jew, and we correctly call him an antisemite. A fanatic spits at a Christian in Jerusalem, and suddenly we are invited to diagnose Israeli society.

That is not analysis. It is a double standard.

If you genuinely want to know whether Christians are flourishing in a country, there are better measures than the behavior of its worst citizens.

Start with the most basic question:

Are Christians disappearing?

In Israel, they are not.

DISPUTE OVER CHRISTIAN GROUPS' VISAS TO ISRAEL RESOLVED AFTER HUCKABEE THREAT

In 1950, Israel was home to roughly 34,000 Christians. Today there are about 184,000, and the community continues to grow.

Then look at what Christians actually do here.

Consider one image that tells you more about Christian integration than a hundred government brochures.

Justice Salim Joubran was an Arab Christian justice of Israel's Supreme Court. He sat on the panel that sent former Israeli president Moshe Katsav to prison. Think about that sentence. An Arab Christian judge helped send the Jewish president of the Jewish state to prison.

And nobody in Israel regarded his ethnicity or religion as an issue. He was a Supreme Court justice doing his job. That is the point.

Christians are physicians and hospital directors, academics and businesspeople, mayors, police officers, soldiers and diplomats.

I happen to be one of them.

The boy from the Christian Scouts in Jaffa eventually joined Israel's diplomatic service and became the first Christian appointed to represent Israel as an ambassador.

Today, I serve as Israel's special envoy to the Christian World, a position created specifically to deepen Israel's relationship with Christian communities around the world. Quite an elaborate way for a country supposedly hostile to Christianity to behave.

There are other inconvenient facts. In 2014, Israel formally recognized the Aramean nationality, giving members of ancient Aramaic and Syriac Christian traditions official recognition of an identity rooted in Christianity's earliest history.

Israel is also investing in Christianity's past and future here.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH SECRET CHURCH TIED TO COUNCIL OF NICAEA, CHRISTIANITY'S DEFINING MOMENT

A few days ago, I visited the excavations at Bethsaida on the Sea of Galilee, where archaeologists identified what is likely to have been the hometown of the Apostles Peter and Andrew.

I watched Israeli and American archaeologists, Jews and Christians, literally digging the world of Jesus back out of the earth.

There is something wonderfully inconvenient about that image: The country supposedly erasing Christianity is uncovering the village of the Apostles.

And Israel is already preparing for 2030, when Christians will mark 2,000 years since the baptism of Jesus, an anniversary expected to bring enormous numbers of pilgrims to the Holy Land.

Something interesting is happening beyond Israel's borders as well. Recent polling in Lebanon found strong support among its Christian communities for peace with Israel: 77% among Maronites and 72% among Orthodox Christians.

Perhaps Middle Eastern Christians, after watching what has happened to ancient communities in Iraq, Syria and elsewhere, are beginning to ask questions that old political slogans cannot answer.

Perhaps Jews and Christians in this region have more invested in one another's survival than generations of conflict allowed either side to admit.

None of this excuses a single act of anti-Christian hatred. A Jew who spits at a priest because he is Christian should be ashamed of himself, and Israel should make sure the law deals with him. Full stop.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Israel has work to do. Enforcement must be stronger. Religious leaders must be louder. Education must be better. I am working inside government on precisely these issues.

But I refuse to give the extremist a promotion. He is an extremist. He does not get promoted to spokesman for ten million Israelis simply because that makes for a more dramatic story.

And yet that is effectively what some of the current coverage does.

The extremist is representative, while the Christian Supreme Court justice is an exception.

How convenient. This works because a distorted picture does not require invented facts. It requires only a carefully chosen frame. Photograph one crack in a cathedral closely enough, and you can make the entire building appear to be collapsing. The crack is real. The picture is false.

item.title: Deadly disease outbreak kills 2,000 as experts reveal what Americans should know
item.description: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed over 2,000 people, but experts say the average American faces very little threat.
item.content:encoded:
As the death toll from the latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) surpasses 2,000 people, infectious disease experts say Americans should remain aware of the humanitarian crisis overseas while understanding the reality of domestic risk.

The virus has spread rapidly across parts of eastern and northeastern DRC, with earlier cross-border cases in Uganda. Published government data shows a total of 4,381 confirmed cases.

"There's a lot of people who live there. So this is not breaking out in a town of 50, but in rural cities of hundreds of thousands," David Wohl, MD, a professor of medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told Fox News Digital.

FAUCI TEXTS SUGGEST OFFICIALS WERE ‘TOO SLOW TO PIVOT' AMID PANDEMIC, SAYS DR MARC SIEGEL

"Compared to previous outbreaks, the pace at which this is moving is unprecedented," he went on. "The slope is just so catastrophic, with more and more people getting infected at a very significant pace without much slowing down."

Controlling transmission has proven particularly difficult in the DRC due to what Wohl calls a "perfect storm" of adverse conditions.

MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL

Dense populations and limited access can complicate efforts to deliver medical care, track contacts and establish quarantine protocols, he noted.

"There's conflict in and around these areas, which makes getting in and out of them … really tough," Wohl said.

Despite the escalating death toll in Africa, health officials emphasize that the average American faces very little threat from Ebola.

"This is not something that I think the average person has to worry about acquiring here in the United States," Wohl said, noting that transmission requires close physical contact with bodily fluids from a severely ill or deceased individual.

"It doesn’t travel across the air and across a room," he added.

Even during the massive 2014 West Africa outbreak, which Wohl said infected more than 28,000 people, only four Ebola cases were diagnosed in the U.S. Two were imported cases, and two nurses contracted the virus while caring for an infected patient in Dallas, according to the CDC. 

Several other Ebola patients who had been infected and diagnosed overseas were medically evacuated to the U.S. for treatment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We just have so much better public health, healthcare systems, hygiene, access," Wohl said. "It's a very different environment."

Viruses like measles, influenza, RSV and SARS-CoV-2 pose more immediate public health concerns for Americans, he added.

"The average person who gets a headache or a fever does not need to worry about Ebola," the doctor said.

For the U.S., potential concerns include the risk to healthcare providers traveling to Africa to assist with containment efforts and the possibility of further instability in the region.

Medical researchers are also navigating challenges with virus variants, according to Wohl.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

While treatments and vaccines were successfully deployed against the Zaire strain during the 2014 crisis, the doctor said the Bundibugyo virus circulating in parts of the DRC is genetically different. 

As a result, approved Ebola therapeutics are not approved for Bundibugyo-related disease, and their effectiveness against it has not been established.

Researchers are actively evaluating new treatments and vaccine candidates for Bundibugyo virus, Wohl said. 

Emerging technologies, including mRNA platforms, could potentially help researchers more rapidly develop vaccines against specific viral threats, according to the doctor.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Global agencies, including the World Health Organization and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, continue to monitor the region closely. Wohl emphasized that international support and resource deployment remain critical to stopping the surge.

"This is a fire that’s raging that continues to be out of control," Wohl said. "There’s lots of people suffering ... and I think more can be done."

item.title: Sophie Cunningham, Caitlin Clark respond to Fever coach Stephanie White's pregame rant
item.description: Caitlin Clark said she felt "sick" when fans booed Stephanie White before the Indiana Fever's 106-92 win over the New York Liberty on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham addressed a viral pre-game rant by their head coach after the Indiana Fever's 106-92 win over the New York Liberty on Tuesday.

Fever coach Stephanie White dedicated her entire pre-game media availability to delivering a rant in defense of herself after she faced criticism for her response on Saturday to an incident when Chicago Sky player DiJonai Carrington smacked Cunningham in the face.

White initially told reporters Saturday that she didn't believe the hit was intentional, before declaring Tuesday that after watching footage, she believed the hit was "egregious."

Cunningham showed support for White after Tuesday's win.

FEVER SHUT DOWN SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM QUESTIONS, ABRUPTLY END PRESS CONFERENCE

"There's just been a lot of outside noise," Cunningham said. "But our locker room is good."

"Our locker room in there, it's tight, and we have each other's backs," she said. "Coach loves us."

Cunningham even defended White's first comments about the foul. White had praised Carrington's competitive nature after the game while agreeing with the officials' decision to eject her. Cunningham said White lacked a full view of the play when she spoke.

"She didn't see the clip," Cunningham said. "At the end of the day, she didn't see the clip."

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT AGAINST DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER FLAGRANT FOUL AND 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

White said Tuesday of the hit, "I didn't see the play in real time. I went straight to a press conference. I thought the play got called right. Thankfully, Sophie's okay. Was it egregious? Absolutely. When you have a chance to watch that over and over and over on replay, you can see that. I didn't have that in real time."

Cunningham noted that White coached Carrington for two seasons with the Connecticut Sun. She said White could recognize Carrington's ability and still support her own player. Cunningham did not view White's comments as a betrayal.

"She is a hell of a player. She's a great defender," Cunningham said of Carrington. "Give her her flowers, and she didn't see it. And that's OK."

Cunningham then removed any doubt about her relationship with White.

"Me and Steph are great," she said. "Steph is great with all of us."

WHY YOU SHOULD BACK THE INDIANA FEVER TO COVER THE SPREAD AGAINST THE NEW YORK LIBERTY TUESDAY

Cunningham then shifted attention back to basketball. She said she no longer worried about the outside reaction.

"I really don't care anymore," Cunningham said. "I'm trying to keep the main thing the main thing."

Cunningham said the Fever shared the ball, defended well and found their joy again.

"With everything going on, that's kind of been hard to do," Cunningham said. "Tonight was the night that we all just, like, clicked, and we had fun, and we did it for Steph, and we did it for everyone in the locker room."

Clark offered a more personal defense. She spoke with White earlier that day and understood the toll of constant criticism.

"I think we forget a lot of times, like, we're human and she has feelings," Clark said. "There's moments that are really hard."

Clark drew from her own experience under intense scrutiny. She told White that even thick skin has limits.

"I've been through the same thing," Clark said. "There's been days where I've been really upset, and you can have the thickest skin in the world, but sometimes it does get to you."

Clark also criticized the broader climate around the team and the league. She said too many people look for conflict instead of celebrating success.

"Our world is just like, we love to hate. We love to divide," Clark said. "Nobody wants to see each other succeed."

Clark called that painful to watch. She said, "We need to do a better job at uplifting each other."

Clark said that she told White that the Fever would deliver a win for her on Tuesday.

FEVER COACH UNLOADS ON WNBA OVER TREATMENT OF CAITLIN CLARK, BUT IT'S TIME FOR CLARK TO START PUNCHING BACK

"I can assure you there was no way we were losing this game tonight," Clark said. "And I told her that before the game. Like, there was no way we were losing this game for her."

Clark also addressed the boos White heard during pregame introductions. She accepted that fans can criticize a coach but found the reaction difficult to hear.

"I hated that our fans booed her before the game," Clark said. "That made me a little sick, to be honest."

Clark said disagreement would not change the players' loyalty. She called White their head coach and said the Fever would protect the unity they had built.

"We're going to ride for her, and we're always going to have her back," Clark said. "That's never going to tear our locker room apart."

She closed by expressing affection for White and pride in the Fever's response. Clark said the team played with energy, shared the ball and competed with smiles on their faces.

"I just love her, and I feel for her because I know it can be a lot at times," Clark said. "We really just did it for her, and we did it for each other and the girls in our locker room."

White's pregame rant on Tuesday also made reference to "hate" and "divisive" forces, without referencing anyone directly, that are apparently trying to "hijack" the league.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said.

"Every day, these women put their a** on the line. Every day. When they go low, we go high. Love will win, grace will win. Humility will win and kindness will win. I stand by them, I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

The WNBA has been at the center of a national controversy for months now, with the Fever being a recurring constant in that controversy. It started when Phoenix Mercury player Alyssa Thomas punched Clark in the throat. It escalated when Cunningham's stance on protecting women's sports was revealed and prompted a national debate on the issue with White and other coaches being mocked for their answers on the issue.

It boiled over on Saturday after Carrington struck Cunningham and then wrote "White privilege" on Threads right after being ejected.

Now, White will try to lead the Fever through that controversy all the way to the playoffs, as the Fever are one of the hottest teams in the league and are in the driver's seat to clinch the top seed in the East.

item.title: Mike Vrabel is finally asked about his family counseling sessions made necessary by the Dianna Russini scandal
item.description: Mike Vrabel deflected a question about his family counseling sessions by pivoting to talk of offensive line combination blocks during New England Patriots camp.
item.content:encoded:
It took weeks since the New England Patriots opened their 2026 training camp and NFL rules put coach Mike Vrabel in front of reporters on a regular basis, but the question finally came on Tuesday.

Someone asked Vrabel what he learned from his counseling sessions that he previously said he was seeking after the scandal involving him and NFL reporter Dianna Russini became public.

Vrabel had announced in April he was following up difficult conversations with his family with that counseling because the photos of him and Russini hugging and holding hands and enjoying time together at a pool and spa doubtless caused friction at home.

PATRIOTS COACH MIKE VRABEL BREAKS SILENCE ON DIANNA RUSSINI PHOTOS THAT LED TO 'DIFFICULT CONVERSATIONS'

Vrabel even missed one day of the NFL Draft as part of that counseling regimen.

But then, well, radio silence.

Vrabel didn't discuss it. And he was not asked about it by the New England media. Even on the first day of camp when Vrabel faced reporters for the first time in 2026, the subject never came up.

But it did on Tuesday.

MIKE VRABEL UNTOUCHED BY DIANNA RUSSINI SCANDAL AT FIRST PRESS CONFERENCE OF PATRIOTS TRAINING CAMP

Finally.

QUESTION: "You said this offseason that you were seeking counseling. I wanted to follow up on that and see what you learned from that counseling, and how did you balance that personal commitment with getting ready for this season?"

Good work here. Journalism!

Vrabel then opened up and explained how the sessions affected his family relationships.

No he didn't.

VRABEL: "I think we always look at improvement. As we talk about getting ready for the next season, we always look at improvement and ways that we can improve individually and how we can improve as a team. It’s really critical that we continue to do that on and off the field.

"I believe in that. I believe in everything that we can do to help this football team, to help our coaches, to help myself and everybody else included.

"This journey that we are going to go on is going to be completely different than the one we went on last year. That’s all of our jobs, is to prepare for it now. So, really focused on our improvement individually and as a team, and that’s something that we can do today.

"You look at the O-line, and we talk about them and their ability to play together as a unit. There are so many combination blocks that they are involved in, and we have to be better. Again, five O-linemen have to be able to sustain a line of scrimmage, and I just walked into that meeting room and said, "How do we improve? How do we improve our combination blocks?

"We are not asking you to block everybody 1-on-1. So, I think we all have areas that we can improve on, and that includes the coaches."

That's a lot of words. But it's not anything close to insightful. Or personal.

The question about Vrabel's family counseling sessions that followed an embarrassing unfurling of a years-long relationship between him and a reporter was met with an answer that ultimately discussed offensive line combination blocks.

This doesn't make Vrabel a bad guy.

Or a bad coach.

That time he spent with the woman not his wife might, but not this. This makes him excellent at coachspeak. And expert in the art of deflection.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

It's understandable because Vrabel is wise to give an answer that does not lead to a follow-up question on an uncomfortable subject. He doesn't want to dredge up any new stories that might cause his team even the slightest distraction.

He wants a story that went viral in the spring to die this summer.

One more thing: He probably doesn't feel like he owes anyone an actual answer.

And he's correct. It's a personal matter for him and he has a right to keep it locked up.

But the question needed to be asked.

Finally, score one for journalism.
